explanations.answer: All the sons of the king
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The text says Absalom, David's son, invited all the sons of the king. That means every brother, Amnon included. A sheepshearing party with the whole royal family on the list, and I think that's a lot of mules to park.

That's a big guest list, but this invitation stays in the family. The text says Absalom invited all the sons of the king. Think brothers, not city council. Nobody in this passage is handing out name tags to elders.
Whole tribe of Judah? That's a stadium crowd, baker. Absalom keeps it smaller, because he invited all the sons of the king. The brothers are the ones getting the invitations.

Close, but the text says the opposite. Absalom asks, “Will the king and his servants please come with me?” The servants are on the invitation too. He asks for the whole royal crew, not a quiet table for one.

Right, because the servants are invited too. Absalom says, “Will the king and his servants please come with me?” He asks for the king and the whole household. The man is not trying to keep the crowd small.

explanations.answer: They would be a burden to Absalom
explanations.explanation: You got it. David says, “…we should not all go, or we would be a burden to you.” He's thinking of the host. Picture the bill for feeding a king and his whole household. I'd say no too, and I can't even afford the sprinkles.

explanations.answer: The road to Baal-hazor is too long
explanations.explanation: David never says a word about the road. What he says is, “…we should not all go, or we would be a burden to you.” His reason is about being a burden to Absalom, not about the miles. Nobody checks the map in this passage.

explanations.answer: He has business at the palace
explanations.explanation: That's a classic excuse, baker, and we've all used it. But David doesn't use it here. He says, “…we should not all go, or we would be a burden to you.” His reason is the burden on Absalom, not a full calendar.

Yes, Amnon. Absalom says, “If not… please let my brother Amnon go with us.” Amnon is David's oldest son, and the text has already told us about what he did to Tamar. Absalom is asking for that one by name.
Solomon was David's son, born to David and Bathsheba (2 Samuel 12:24). But he isn't the brother Absalom asks for here. Absalom says, “…please let my brother Amnon go with us.”
Adonijah was another son of David, born to Haggith (2 Samuel 3:4). He's not in this ask, though. Absalom says, “…please let my brother Amnon go with us.” Amnon is the name he gives.

explanations.answer: Why should he go with you
explanations.explanation: That's the one. David asks, “Why should he go with you?” I think that question just sits there in the air for a second. David doesn't say more about it, and Absalom keeps pressing.
David doesn't ask about Amnon's feelings on the trip. The king asks, “Why should he go with you?” He's asking Absalom, not checking Amnon's schedule.
Good question for a party, but David doesn't ask it. He asks, “Why should he go with you?” He wants to know why Amnon, not who else is coming. Only one brother is under the spotlight here.

explanations.answer: Until Amnon's heart is merry with wine
explanations.explanation: That's the heavy part of this passage. Absalom orders, “Watch Amnon until his heart is merry with wine…” The young men are waiting for that moment and for Absalom's signal. I think this is a hard one to read.

explanations.answer: Until Amnon falls asleep in his tent
explanations.explanation: A tent never comes up in the text. Absalom says, “Watch Amnon until his heart is merry with wine…” The signal is about the wine, not a nap. It's a heavy part of the story, so we'll keep it straight.

explanations.answer: Until the last sheep has been sheared
explanations.explanation: The sheep are the reason for the party, but they aren't the timer here. Absalom says, “Watch Amnon until his heart is merry with wine…” The young men are watching Amnon, not the flock. This part of the story is heavy, so I'll stick to what the text says.

Yes, he does. Absalom tells them, “Do not be afraid. Have I not commanded you? Be courageous and valiant!” That's an order to kill a king's son, and I think it's hard to read. He's pushing them to go through with it.

The text says the opposite. Absalom tells his young men, “Do not be afraid. Have I not commanded you? Be courageous and valiant!” He's ordering them to strike down a son of the king. This is a heavy moment, and I think it hurts to read.

explanations.answer: Each one flees on his mule
explanations.explanation: That's right. The text says, “…each one fled on his mule.” It's not the fastest getaway, but it's what they had. They got up and left in a hurry, and nobody stayed to find out what happened next.
No swords come out in the text. It says all the other sons of the king got up, and “each one fled on his mule.” They ran for the road, not for a fight.
Mourning comes later, baker, and it comes in a different place. Here the other sons of the king got up, and “each one fled on his mule.” Nobody sits down at the party.

explanations.answer: Absalom has struck down all the king's sons
explanations.explanation: That's the report. David hears, “Absalom has struck down all the sons of the king; not one of them is left!” Notice the report says ALL of them. We're about to find out it isn't true.

explanations.answer: Amnon has struck down his brother Absalom
explanations.explanation: That's backwards, friend. The report says Absalom did the striking. David hears, “Absalom has struck down all the sons of the king; not one of them is left!” Amnon is not the one doing anything in that report.

explanations.answer: Robbers have attacked the king's sons
explanations.explanation: Robbers aren't in the story at all. The report names Absalom: “Absalom has struck down all the sons of the king; not one of them is left!” The news is about a brother, and that makes it heavier.

True. The text says, “Then the king stood up, tore his clothes, and lay down on the ground.” Tearing the clothes shows how hard the news hits him. It's what a father does when he thinks he's lost everything.
Not quite. The text says, “Then the king stood up, tore his clothes, and lay down on the ground.” He does tear them. And his servants stand by with their clothes torn too.
Yes, and Jonadab, the son of David's brother Shimeah, says it plainly: “…only Amnon is dead.” The first report said all the sons were gone. Jonadab corrects it with one name.
Absalom is alive, friend. He's the one who ordered this and then fled. Jonadab, David's nephew, says, “…only Amnon is dead.”
I wish that were the case, baker. But Jonadab, the son of David's brother Shimeah, says, “…only Amnon is dead.” It's better than all the sons, but it's still a death, and it's heavy.

explanations.answer: Since the day Amnon violated Tamar
explanations.explanation: That's what Jonadab says: “…Absalom has planned this since the day Amnon violated his sister Tamar.” That's two years of waiting. Nobody had to tell him the reason, because Jonadab says it outright.

explanations.answer: Since the day the shearers were hired
explanations.explanation: That's closer in time, but it's not what the text says. Jonadab says, “…Absalom has planned this since the day Amnon violated his sister Tamar.” The plan goes back further than the party.

explanations.answer: Since the day David blessed him
explanations.explanation: David did bless Absalom in this story, but the plan is older. Jonadab says, “…Absalom has planned this since the day Amnon violated his sister Tamar.” The blessing didn't start anything.
Careful, baker. Jonadab doesn't say that. He says, “Look, the sons of the king have arrived! It is just as your servant said.” The people coming are the king's sons, not Absalom's young men.

Right. Jonadab says, “Look, the sons of the king have arrived! It is just as your servant said.” The watchman sees men coming, and Jonadab says they're the king's sons. They're coming home, not coming for anyone.

That's what the text says. “And as he finished speaking, the sons of the king came in, wailing loudly.” Jonadab had just said it, and there they are, alive. Then the king and all his servants weep very bitterly too.

The text says it happened just that way. “And as he finished speaking, the sons of the king came in, wailing loudly.” They did come in, and Jonadab's words came true right on cue. It's a heavy scene, with everyone weeping.
That's the word. The text says, “But David mourned for his son every day.” Not one day, every day. I think that's a father who is hurting.
The text doesn't say he went searching. It says, “But David mourned for his son every day.” Mourning is what David does here, and it keeps going.
No watching in this verse. A watchman does show up earlier in this passage, but David isn't the one. The text says, “But David mourned for his son every day.”
Yes, three years. The text says, “After Absalom had fled and gone to Geshur, he stayed there three years.” That's a long time to be away from home. Geshur is where Talmai, its king, lived.
Seven is a big number in the Bible, but not in this verse. The text says Absalom “stayed there three years.” Geshur holds him for three.
Forty days is a short stay compared to this one. The text says Absalom “stayed there three years.” That's years, not days, and it's a long time to be gone.

True. The text says, “And King David longed to go to Absalom, for he had been consoled over Amnon’s death.” The grief has eased, and now he longs for the son who ran. I think that's a father's heart at work.

The text says the opposite, friend. “And King David longed to go to Absalom, for he had been consoled over Amnon’s death.” His heart turns toward the son who fled. I think there's a lot of hurt tied up in that longing.
